arXiv:1709.06192v1 [math.AP] 18 Sep 2017

Asymptotic behavior of Boussinesq system of KdV-KdV type

R. A. Capistrano–Filho Address: Departamento de Matemática, Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, 50740-545, Recife-PE, Brazil. Email address: capistranofilho@dmat.ufpe.br and F. A. Gallego Address: Departamento de Matemáticas y Estadística, Universidad Nacional de Colombia - Sede Manizales, Colombia Email address: fagallegor@unal.edu.co
Abstract.

This work deals with the local rapid exponential stabilization for a Boussinesq system of KdV-KdV type introduced by J. Bona, M. Chen and J.-C. Saut. This is a model for the motion of small amplitude long waves on the surface of an ideal fluid. Here, we will consider the Boussinesq system of KdV-KdV type posed on a finite domain, with homogeneous Dirichlet–Neumann boundary controls acting at the right end point of the interval. Our goal is to build suitable integral transformations to get a feedback control law that leads to the stabilization of the system. More precisely, we will prove that the solution of the closed-loop system decays exponentially to zero in the L2​(0,L)L^{2}(0,L)–norm and the decay rate can be tuned to be as large as desired if the initial data is small enough.

Key words and phrases: 
Boussinesq system KdV–KdV type, stabilization, feedback integral transformation, backstepping method
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
Primary: 93B05, 93D15, 35Q53

1. Introduction

1.1. Setting of the problem

The classical Boussinesq systems were first derived by Boussinesq in [4], to describe the two-way propagation of small amplitude, long wave length gravity waves on the surface of water in a canal. These systems and their higher-order generalizations also arise when modeling the propagation of long-crested waves on large lakes or on the ocean and in other contexts. Recently, in [2], the authors derived a four-parameter family of Boussinesq systems to describe the motion of small amplitude long waves on the surface of an ideal fluid under the gravity force and in situations where the motion is sensibly two dimensional. More precisely, they studied a family of systems of the form

(1.1) {ηt+wx+(η​w)x+a​wx​x​x−b​ηx​x​t=0​,wt+ηx+w​wx+c​ηx​x​x−d​wx​x​t=0​.\left\{\begin{array}[c]{l}\eta_{t}+w_{x}+(\eta w)_{x}+aw_{xxx}-b\eta_{xxt}=0\text{,}\\ w_{t}+\eta_{x}+ww_{x}+c\eta_{xxx}-dw_{xxt}=0\text{.}\end{array}\right.

In (1.1), η\eta is the elevation from the equilibrium position, and w=wθw=w_{\theta} is the horizontal velocity in the flow at height θ​h\theta h, where hh is the undisturbed depth of the liquid. The parameters aa, bb, cc, dd, that one might choose in a given modeling situation, are required to fulfill the relations

(1.2) a+b=12​(θ2−13)​, ​c+d=12​(1−θ2)≥0​, ​θ∈[0,1],a+b=\frac{1}{2}\left(\theta^{2}-\frac{1}{3}\right)\text{, \ \ \ }c+d=\frac{1}{2}(1-\theta^{2})\geq 0\text{, \ \ \ }\theta\in\left[0,1\right],

where θ∈[0,1]\theta\in\left[0,1\right] specifies which horizontal velocity the variable ww represents (cf. [2]). Consequently,

a+b+c+d=13.a+b+c+d=\frac{1}{3}.

As it has been proved in [2], the initial value problem for the linear system associated with (1.1) is well-posed on ℝ\mathbb{R} if either C1C_{1} or C2C_{2} is satisfied, where

(C1)\displaystyle(C_{1}) b,d≥0,a≤0,c≤0;\displaystyle b,d\geq 0,\ a\leq 0,\ c\leq 0;
(C2)\displaystyle(C_{2}) b,d≥0,a=c>0.\displaystyle b,d\geq 0,\ a=c>0.

When b=d=0b=d=0 and (C2)(C_{2}) is satisfied, then necessarily a=c=1/6a=c=1/6. Nevertheless, the scaling x→x/6x\to x/\sqrt{6}, t→t/6t\to t/\sqrt{6} gives an system equivalent to (1.1) for which a=c=1a=c=1, namely

(1.3) {ηt+wx+wx​x​x+(η​w)x=0,in​(0,L)×(0,+∞),wt+ηx+ηx​x​x+w​wx=0,in​(0,L)×(0,+∞),η(x,0)=η0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),in​(0,L),\begin{cases}\eta_{t}+w_{x}+w_{xxx}+(\eta w)_{x}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,+\infty),\\ w_{t}+\eta_{x}+\eta_{xxx}+ww_{x}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,+\infty),\\ \eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x),\quad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),&\text{in}\,\,(0,L),\end{cases}

which is the so-called Boussinesq system of Korteweg-de Vries—Korteweg-de Vries type.

Therefore, the interest of this work is to give a positive answer for the following stabilization problem:

 

Problem 𝒜\mathcal{A}: Can one find a linear feedback control law

(f⁡(t),g⁡(t))=F⁡[(η⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))],t∈(0,∞),(f(t),g(t))=F[(\eta(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))],\quad t\in(0,\infty),

such that the closed-loop system (1.3) with boundary condition

(1.4) {η(0,t)=0,η(L,t)=0,ηx(0,t)=f(t),t∈(0,∞),w(0,t)=0,w(L,t)=0,wx(L,t)=g(t),t∈(0,∞)\begin{cases}\eta(0,t)=0,\,\,\eta(L,t)=0,\,\,\eta_{x}(0,t)=f(t),&t\in(0,\infty),\\ w(0,t)=0,\,\,w(L,t)=0,\,\,w_{x}(L,t)=g(t),&t\in(0,\infty)\end{cases}

is exponentially stable?

 

As we know, there are some natural methods that may give us a positive answers of the Problem 𝒜\mathcal{A}, e.g., the so-called “Gramian approach” (see [16, 20, 22] and the reference therein for more details), the Lyapunov function method (see, for instance, [7]), and, finally, the backstepping method, that is now a standard method for finite dimensional control systems (see, e.g., [7, 14, 15, 21]). The first adaptations of the backstepping method to control systems modeled by partial differential equations were given in [8] and [13], by using a Volterra transformation [3].

1.2. State of art

In this paper, we will try to apply the backstepping method (see [15] for a systematic introduction of this method) to design the feedback control law. This method was successfully applied by Coron et. al. in [9, 10] to study the rapid stabilization of the Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) and the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky (K–S) equations, respectively.

More precisely, which concerning of KdV equation, in [9], the authors studied the KdV equation on a bounded domain (0,L)(0,L)

(1.5) {ut+u​ux+ux+ux​x​x=0in ​(0,L)×(0,+∞)​,u⁡(0,t)=u⁡(L,t)=0on ​(0,+∞),ux​(L,t)=h​(t)on ​(0,+∞),\left\{\begin{array}[c]{lll}u_{t}+uu_{x}+u_{x}+u_{xxx}=0&&\text{in }(0,L)\times(0,+\infty)\text{,}\\ u(0,t)=u(L,t)=0&&\text{on }(0,+\infty),\\ u_{x}(L,t)=h(t)&&\text{on }(0,+\infty),\end{array}\right.

where the function h⁡(t)=Fλ​(u⁡(t))h(t)=F_{\lambda}(u(t)) is the feedback law designed to ensure the exponential stability of the system with a decay rate equal to λ\lambda. This decay rate can be chosen as large as desired, which is called a rapid stabilization result. They consider the following problem:

 

Problem ℬ\mathcal{B}: Let λ>0\lambda>0. Does there exist a linear feedback control Fλ:L2​(0,L)→ℝF_{\lambda}:L^{2}(0,L)\to\mathbb{R} such that, for some δ>0\delta>0, every solution uu of (1.5) with h⁡(t)=Fλ​(u⁡(⋅,t))h(t)=F_{\lambda}(u(\cdot,t)) satisfies

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​(0,L)≤C​e−λ​t​‖u⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L),||u(\cdot,t)||_{L^{2}(0,L)}\leq Ce^{-\lambda t}||u(\cdot,0)||_{L^{2}(0,L)},

for some C>0C>0, provided that ‖u⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L)≤δ||u(\cdot,0)||_{L^{2}(0,L)}\leq\delta?

 

A positive answer to this question was given in [9] (see also [10] for K–S equation) using a modified backstepping method and the following result was obtained.

 

Theorem A (Coron et al. [9]) For every λ>0\lambda>0, there exist a continuous linear feedback control law F:L2​(0,L)→ℝF:L^{2}(0,L)\to\mathbb{R}, and positive constants r>0r>0 and C>0C>0 such that, for every u0∈L2​(0,L)u^{0}\in L^{2}(0,L) satisfying ‖u0‖L2​(0,L)≤r||u^{0}||_{L^{2}(0,L)}\leq r, the solution vv of (1.5), with h⁡(t):=F⁡(u⁡(⋅,t))h(t):=F(u(\cdot,t)) satisfying the initial condition u⁡(⋅,0)=u0​(⋅)u(\cdot,0)=u^{0}(\cdot), is defined on [0,+∞)[0,+\infty) and satisfies

‖u⁡(⋅,t)‖L2​(0,L)≤C​e−λ2​t​‖u⁡(⋅,0)‖L2​(0,L), for every t≥0.||u(\cdot,t)||_{L^{2}(0,L)}\leq Ce^{-\frac{\lambda}{2}t}||u(\cdot,0)||_{L^{2}(0,L)},\quad\text{ for every }\quad t\geq 0.

The main difficulty to establish Theorem A is the fact that the linear system is known to be non-controllable (and consequently non-stabilizable) if the length of the interval LL belongs to a set of critical values 𝒩\mathcal{N} (see for instance [19]). The authors looked for an integral transform

(1.6) w⁡(x,t)=u⁡(x,t)−∫0Lk⁡(x,y)​u​(y,t)​𝑑yw(x,t)=u(x,t)-\int_{0}^{L}k(x,y)u(y,t)dy

with k=k⁡(x,y)k=k(x,y) chosen such that u=u⁡(x,t)u=u(x,t) is a solution of (1.5) if and only if w=w⁡(x,t)w=w(x,t) is a solution of

(1.7) {wt+wx+wx​x​x+λ​w=−u​ux−12​∫0Lky​(x,y)​u2​(y,t)​dy,w⁡(0,t)=w⁡(L,t)=wx​(L,t)=0.\begin{cases}w_{t}+w_{x}+w_{xxx}+\lambda w=-uu_{x}-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{L}k_{y}(x,y)u^{2}(y,t)dy,\\ w(0,t)=w(L,t)=w_{x}(L,t)=0.\end{cases}

Thus, they proved that the system (1.7) is locally exponentially stable with a decay rate equal to λ\lambda. This result follows for (1.5) if the integral transform (1.6) exists and is invertible and if the kernel function k=k⁡(x,y)k=k(x,y) satisfies a partial differential equation with a Dirac measure as a source term. Is important to see that this result holds if the length LL is not critical.

 

Now, we will come back to the stabilization properties of the system (1.3) on a bounded domain. As far we know, the KdV–KdV system is expected to admit global solutions on ℝ\mathbb{R}, and it also possesses good control properties on the torus [17]. However, there are few results concerning to the bounded domains. The unique result in the literature is due to Pazoto and Rosier in [18]. They investigated the asymptotic behavior of the solutions of the system (1.3) satisfying the boundary conditions

(1.8) {w(0,t)=wx​x(0,t)=0 on (0,T),wx​(0,t)=α0​ηx​(0,t)on (0,T),w⁡(L,t)=α2​η​(L,t)on (0,T),wx​(L,t)=−α1​ηx​(L,t)on (0,T),wx​x​(L,t)=−α2​ηx​x​(L,t)on (0,T)\left\{\begin{array}[c]{lll}w(0,t)=w_{xx}(0,t)=0\text{ }&&\text{on $(0,T)$,}\\ w_{x}(0,t)=\alpha_{0}\eta_{x}(0,t)&&\text{on $(0,T)$,}\\ w(L,t)=\alpha_{2}\eta(L,t)&&\text{on $(0,T)$,}\\ w_{x}(L,t)=-\alpha_{1}\eta_{x}(L,t)&&\text{on $(0,T)$,}\\ w_{xx}(L,t)=-\alpha_{2}\eta_{xx}(L,t)&&\text{on $(0,T)$}\end{array}\right.

and initial conditions

(1.9) η⁡(x,0)=η0​(x)​, ​w​(x,0)=w0​(x)on ​(0,L)​.\begin{array}[c]{lll}\eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\text{, \ }w(x,0)=w_{0}(x)&&\text{on }(0,L)\text{.}\end{array}

In (1.8), α0\alpha_{0}, α1\alpha_{1} and α2\alpha_{2} denote some nonnegative real constants.

Under the above boundary conditions, they observed that the derivative of the energy associated to the system (1.3), with boundary conditions (1.8)-(1.9), satisfies

d​Ed​t=−α2​|η⁡(L,t)|2−α1​|ηx​(L,t)|2−α0​|ηx​(0,t)|2−13​w3​(L,t)−∫0L(η​w)x​η​𝑑x,\frac{dE}{dt}=-\alpha_{2}\left|\eta(L,t)\right|^{2}-\alpha_{1}\left|\eta_{x}(L,t)\right|^{2}-\alpha_{0}\left|\eta_{x}(0,t)\right|^{2}-\frac{1}{3}w^{3}(L,t)-\int_{0}^{L}(\eta w)_{x}\eta dx,

where

E⁡(t)=12​∫0L(η2+w2)​𝑑x​.E(t)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{L}(\eta^{2}+w^{2})dx\text{.}

This indicates that the boundary conditions play the role of a feedback damping mechanism, at least for the linearized system. Therefore, the following questions arise:

 

Problem 𝒞\mathcal{C}: Does E⁡(t)→0E(t)\rightarrow 0, as t→+∞​?t\rightarrow+\infty? If it is the case, can we give the decay rate?

 

The problem might be easy to solve when the underlying model has a intrinsic dissipative nature. Moreover, in the context of coupled systems, in order to achieve the desired decay property, the damping mechanism has to be designed in an appropriate way in order to capture all the components of the system. The main result of [18] provides a positive answer to those questions.

 

Theorem B (Pazoto et al. [18]) Assume that α0≥0\alpha_{0}\geq 0, α1>0\alpha_{1}>0 and α2=1\alpha_{2}=1. Then there exist some numbers ρ>0\rho>0, C>0C>0 and μ>0\mu>0 such that for any (η0,w0)∈(L2​(I))2(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in(L^{2}(I))^{2} with

‖(η0,w0)‖(L2​(I))2≤ρ​,\left\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\right\|_{(L^{2}(I))^{2}}\leq\rho\text{,}

the system (1.3)-(1.9) admits a unique solution

(η,w)∈C⁡(ℝ+,(L2​(I))2)∩C⁡(ℝ+⁣∗,(H1​(I))2)∩L2​(0,1,(H1​(I))2)​,(\eta,w)\in C(\mathbb{R}^{+};(L^{2}(I))^{2})\cap C(\mathbb{R}^{+\ast};(H^{1}(I))^{2})\cap L^{2}(0,1;(H^{1}(I))^{2})\text{,}

which fulfills

‖(η,w)​(t)‖(L2​(I))2≤C​e−μ​t​‖(η0,w0)‖(L2​(I))2​, ​∀t≥0​,\left\|(\eta,w)(t)\right\|_{(L^{2}(I))^{2}}\leq Ce^{-\mu t}\left\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\right\|_{(L^{2}(I))^{2}}\text{, }\forall t\geq 0\text{,}
‖(η,w)​(t)‖(H1​(I))2≤C​e−μ​tt​‖(η0,w0)‖(L2​(I))2​, ​∀t>0​.\left\|(\eta,w)(t)\right\|_{(H^{1}(I))^{2}}\leq C\frac{e^{-\mu t}}{\sqrt{t}}\left\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\right\|_{(L^{2}(I))^{2}}\text{, }\forall t>0\text{.}

In our case, we propose to use the ideas contained in [9] to obtain a positive answer for the Problem 𝒜\mathcal{A}. However, first, we need to know a answer for the the following exact controllability problem.

 

Problem 𝒟\mathcal{D}: Given T>0T>0 and (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0}), (ηT,wT)(\eta_{T},w_{T}) in certain space, can one find appropriate f⁡(t)f(t) and g⁡(t)g(t), in a certain space, such that the corresponding solution (η,w)(\eta,w) of the linearized system

(1.10) {ηt+wx+wx​x​x=0in ​(0,L)×(0,T)​,wt+ηx+ηx​x​x=0in ​(0,L)×(0,T)​,\left\{\begin{array}[c]{lll}\eta_{t}+w_{x}+w_{xxx}=0&&\text{in }(0,L)\times(0,T)\text{,}\\ w_{t}+\eta_{x}+\eta_{xxx}=0&&\text{in }(0,L)\times(0,T)\text{,}\end{array}\right.

with the boundary conditions

(1.11) {η⁡(0,t)=η⁡(L,t)=0​, ​ηx​(0,t)=f⁡(t)on ​(0,T)​,w⁡(0,t)=w⁡(L,t)=0​, ​wx​(L,t)=g⁡(t)on ​(0,T)\left\{\begin{array}[c]{lll}\eta(0,t)=\eta(L,t)=0\text{, }\eta_{x}(0,t)=f(t)&&\text{on }(0,T)\text{,}\\ w(0,t)=w(L,t)=0\text{, }w_{x}(L,t)=g(t)&&\text{on }(0,T)\end{array}\right.

and the initial conditions

(1.12) η⁡(x,0)=η0​(x)​, ​w​(x,0)=w0​(x)in ​(0,L)​.\begin{array}[c]{lll}\eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x)\text{, \ }w(x,0)=w_{0}(x)&&\text{in }(0,L)\text{.}\end{array}

satisfies η⁡(⋅,T)=ηT\eta(\cdot,T)=\eta_{T} and w⁡(⋅,T)=wTw(\cdot,T)=w_{T}?

 

More recently, in [6] (see also [5]), the exact boundary controllability of the linear system Boussinesq of KdV–KdV type was studied. It was discovered that whether the associated linear system is exactly controllable or not depends on the length of the spatial domain. In the context of equations that possess a hyperbolic structure, recent results deals with systems of two wave-type equations, only one of them being directly damped. More precisely, the following result was obtained for the system (1.10)-(1.12).

 

Theorem C (Capistrano–Filho et al. [6]) Let

(1.13) 𝒩:={2​π3k2+k​l+l2:k,l∈ℕ∗}.\mathcal{N}:=\left\{\frac{2\pi}{\sqrt{3}}\sqrt{k^{2}+kl+l^{2}}\,:k,\,l\,\in\mathbb{N}^{\ast}\right\}.

For any T>0T>0, L∈(0,+∞)\𝒩L\in(0,+\infty)\backslash\mathcal{N}, (η0,w0)∈[H−1​(0,L)]2(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in[H^{-1}(0,L)]^{2} and (ηT,wT)∈[H−1​(0,L)]2(\eta_{T},w_{T})\in[H^{-1}(0,L)]^{2}, there exist controls (f⁡(t),g⁡(t))∈[L2​(0,T)]2(f(t),g(t))\in[L^{2}(0,T)]^{2} such that the solution (η,w)∈C0​([0,T],[H−1​(0,L)]2)(\eta,w)\in C^{0}([0,T],[H^{-1}(0,L)]^{2}) of (1.10)-(1.12), satisfies η⁡(⋅,T)=ηT\eta(\cdot,T)=\eta_{T} and w⁡(⋅,T)=wTw(\cdot,T)=w_{T}.

 

As in the case of the KdV equation [19, Lemma 3.5] when L∈𝒩L\in\mathcal{N}, the linear system (1.10)-(1.12) is not controllable11 1 There exists a finite-dimensional subspace of L2​(0,L)L^{2}(0,L), denoted by ℳ=ℳ⁡(L)\mathcal{M}=\mathcal{M}(L), which is unreachable from 00 for the linear system.. To prove Theorem C, the authors used the classical duality approach based upon the Hilbert Uniqueness Method (H.U.M.) due to J.-L. Lions [11], which reduces the exact controllability of the system to some observability inequality to be proved for the adjoint system. Then, to establish the required observability inequality, was used the compactness-uniqueness argument due to J.-L. Lions [12] and some multipliers, which reduces the analysis to study a spectral problem. The spectral problem is finally solved by using a method introduced in [19], based on the use of complex analysis, namely, the Paley-Wiener theorem.

With all of these results in hands, we are now in position to present our main result. In this paper, considerations about the local rapid stabilization of the following system

(1.18) {k⁡(x,0)=k⁡(x,L)=k⁡(0,y)=k⁡(L,y)=ky​(x,0)=ky​(x,L)=0,on (0,L),s⁡(x,0)=s⁡(x,L)=s⁡(0,y)=s⁡(L,y)=sy​(x,0)=sy​(x,L)=0,on (0,L),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l }k(x,0)=k(x,L)=k(0,y)=k(L,y)=k_{y}(x,0)=k_{y}(x,L)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\\ s(x,0)=s(x,L)=s(0,y)=s(L,y)=s_{y}(x,0)=s_{y}(x,L)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\end{array}\right.

where λ∈ℝ∖{0}\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} and δ⁡(x−y)\delta(x-y) denotes the Dirac measure on the diagonal of the square [0,L]×[0,L][0,L]\times[0,L]. The definition of a solution to (1.17)-(1.18) is given in Section 3.1. With this system in hands, we are able to prove the following assertions:

  • a.

    System (1.17)-(1.18) has a unique solution;

  • b.

    The operators (I−(K+S))−1(I-(K+S))^{-1} and (I−(K−S))−1(I-(K-S))^{-1} exist and it is a continuous operator in L2​(0,L)L^{2}(0,L), that is, (I−(K+S))−1(I-(K+S))^{-1} and (I−(K−S))−1(I-(K-S))^{-1} belongs to ℒ​(L2​(0,L),ℝ)\mathcal{L}(L^{2}(0,L);\mathbb{R});

  • c.

    Assuming that L∈(0,+∞)\𝒩L\in(0,+\infty)\backslash\mathcal{N}, if we define the feedback law F⁡(⋅)=(F1​(⋅),F2​(⋅))F(\cdot)=(F_{1}(\cdot),F_{2}(\cdot)) by

    f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))=∫0L[kx​(0,y)​η​(y,t)+sx​(0,y)​w​(y,t)]​𝑑y​ on ​(0,T)f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))=\int_{0}^{L}\left[k_{x}(0,y)\eta(y,t)+s_{x}(0,y)w(y,t)\right]dy\text{ on }(0,T)

    and

    g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))=∫0L[kx​(L,y)​w​(y,t)+sx​(L,y)​η​(y,t)]​𝑑y​ on ​(0,T)g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))=\int_{0}^{L}\left[k_{x}(L,y)w(y,t)+s_{x}(L,y)\eta(y,t)\right]dy\text{ on }(0,T)

    then, for the solution (η,w)∈C⁡(ℝ+,X¯2)(\eta,w)\in C(\mathbb{R}^{+};\overline{X}_{2}) of (1.14)-(1.15), one has

    ‖(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))‖X0≤C⁡(‖(I−K)​η​(t)−S​w​(t)‖L2​(0,L)+||(I−K)​w​(t)−S​η​(t)||L2​(0,L)),||(\eta(t),w(t))||_{X_{0}}\leq C\left(||(I-K)\eta(t)-Sw(t)||_{L^{2}(0,L)}+||(I-K)w(t)-S\eta(t)||_{L^{2}(0,L)}\right),

    for some C:=C⁡(K,S)>0C:=C(K,S)>0 depending on the operators KK and SS.

Thus, in order to prove the local exponential stability of (1.14)-(1.15) and since the critical set of the Boussinesq system of KdV–KdV type is defined by (1.13), the above statements are the key to prove the main result of this paper, which can be stated as follows.

Theorem 1.1.

Let T>0T>0 and L∈(0,+∞)\𝒩L\in(0,+\infty)\backslash\mathcal{N}. For every λ>0\lambda>0, there exist a continuous linear feedback control law

F:=(F1,F2):L2​(0,L)×L2​(0,L)→ℝ×ℝ,F:=(F_{1},F_{2}):L^{2}(0,L)\times L^{2}(0,L)\to\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R},

and positive constants ρ∈(0,+∞)\rho\in(0,+\infty) and C:=C⁡(K,S)>0C:=C(K,S)>0, depending on the operators KK and SS, defined by (1.16), such that, for every (η0,w0)∈X¯2(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in\overline{X}_{2} with

‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2<ρ,\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}<\rho,

the solution (η,w)(\eta,w) of (1.14)-(1.15) belongs to space C⁡([0,T],X¯2)C([0,T];\overline{X}_{2}) and satisfies

‖(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))‖X0≤C​e−λ2​t​‖(η0,w0)‖X0,0≤t≤T.\|(\eta(t),w(t))\|_{X_{0}}\leq Ce^{-\frac{\lambda}{2}t}\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{X_{0}},\quad 0\leq t\leq T.
Remarks 1.2.

The following remarks are now in order.

  • (i.)

    In general to propose some stabilization result using standard methods is necessary that the derivative of the energy be negative, see for instance [18]. However, using this approach, namely, backstepping method, the mechanism of damping does not give us any signal of the energy even for the linear system.

  • (ii.)

    Backstepping method is interesting due of the fact that we can deal directly with nonlinear problem instead of first to prove a result for the linear problem and after, using the fixed point argument, to extend for the nonlinear one.

  • (iii.)

    In this work, we can not able to deal with the problem with only one control acting on the boundary conditions, that is, f⁡(t)=0f(t)=0 or g⁡(t)=0g(t)=0 in (1.15). Its looks a interesting problem and we detail the difficulties at the end of this work (see Section 5).

Thus, the plan of the present paper is as follows.

– Section 2 is devoted to study the well-posedness of the system (1.3).

– In the Section 3, we will prove the existence and uniqueness of solution of the stationary problem (1.17)-(1.18).

– The proof of our main result, Theorem 1.1, is made in the Section 4.

– Section 5 is devoted to some remarks and related problems.

2. Well-posedness

In this section, we explain what we mean by a solution of (1.3) and we prove that the non-homogeneous linear system is well-posed.

2.1. Well-posedness: Linear homogeneous system

The result below is related with the existence of solutions of the following linear system

(2.1) {ηt+wx+wx​x​x=0,in​(0,L)×(0,T),wt+ηx+ηx​x​x=0,in​(0,L)×(0,T),η⁡(0,t)=η⁡(L,t)=ηx​(0,t)=0,on​(0,T),w⁡(0,t)=w⁡(L,t)=wx​(L,t)=0,on​d​g​(0,T),η(x,0)=η0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),on​(0,L),\begin{cases}\eta_{t}+w_{x}+w_{xxx}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,T),\\ w_{t}+\eta_{x}+\eta_{xxx}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,T),\\ \eta(0,t)=\eta(L,t)=\eta_{x}(0,t)=0,&\text{on}\,\,(0,T),\\ w(0,t)=w(L,t)=w_{x}(L,t)=0,&\text{on}dg\,\,(0,T),\\ \eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x),\quad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),&\text{on}\,\,(0,L),\\ \end{cases}

and can be found in [6, Proposition 2.1], thus we will omit the proof.

Theorem 2.1.

Let (η0,w0)∈X0(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in X_{0}. Let A⁡(φ,ψ)=(−ψ′−ψ′′′,−φ′−φ′′′)A(\varphi,\psi)=(-\psi^{\prime}-\psi^{\prime\prime\prime},-\varphi^{\prime}-\varphi^{\prime\prime\prime}) with domain D⁡(A)=X¯3D(A)=\overline{X}_{3}. Then, there exists a unique mild solution of (2.1) such that

(η,w)=S⁡(⋅)​(η0,w0)∈C⁡(ℝ+,X0),(\eta,w)=S(\cdot)(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in C(\mathbb{R}^{+};X_{0}),

where S⁡(⋅)S(\cdot) is a group of isometries in X0X_{0} generated by operator AA. Moreover, if (η0,w0)∈D⁡(A)(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in D(A), then (2.1) has a unique (classical) solution (η,w)(\eta,w) belongs to C⁡(ℝ+,D⁡(A))∩C1​(ℝ+,X0)C(\mathbb{R}^{+};D(A))\cap C^{1}(\mathbb{R}^{+};X_{0}).

Using Theorem 2.1 combined with some interpolation argument between X¯0\overline{X}_{0} and X¯3\overline{X}_{3}, we infer for any s∈[0,3]s\in[0,3], there exists a constant Cs>0C_{s}>0 such that for any (η0,w0)∈X¯s(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in\overline{X}_{s}, the solution (η,w)(\eta,w) of (2.1) satisfies (η,w)∈C⁡(ℝ,X¯s)(\eta,w)\in C(\mathbb{R};\overline{X}_{s}) and

(2.2) ‖(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))‖X¯s≤Cs​‖(η0,w0)‖X¯s,∀t∈ℝ,\|(\eta(t),w(t))\|_{\overline{X}_{s}}\leq C_{s}\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{s}},\quad\forall t\in\mathbb{R},

for instance, see [6] for more details.

2.2. Well-posedness: Nonlinear system

We are now in position of to prove the well-posedness for the nonlinear system (1.14)-(1.15), where f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)), with FiF_{i} belongs to ℒ⁡(X0,ℝ)\mathcal{L}(X_{0};\mathbb{R}), i=1,2i=1,2. The following theorem can be proved.

Theorem 2.2.

Let Fi:X0⟶ℝF_{i}:X_{0}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} be a continuous linear map for i=1,2i=1,2 and T>0T>0. Then, there exists ρ>0\rho>0 such that, for every (η0,w0)∈X¯2(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in\overline{X}_{2} satisfying

‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2<ρ,\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}<\rho,

there exists a unique solution (η,w)∈C⁡([0,T],X¯2)(\eta,w)\in C([0,T];\overline{X}_{2}) of (1.14)-(1.15) with f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)). Moreover

‖(η,w)‖C⁡([0,T],X¯2)≤C​‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2\displaystyle\|(\eta,w)\|_{C([0,T];\overline{X}_{2})}\leq C\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}

for some positive constant C=C⁡(T)C=C(T).

The next result establish the well-posedness of the non-homogeneous feedback linear system associated to (2.3).

Lemma 2.4.

Let T>0T>0 and Fi:X0⟶ℝF_{i}:X_{0}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} be a continuous bilinear map, for i=1,2i=1,2. Then, for every (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0}) in X¯2\overline{X}_{2} and (h1,h2)∈L2​(0,T,X−1)(h_{1},h_{2})\in L^{2}(0,T;X_{-1}), there exists a unique solution (η,w)(\eta,w) of the system (2.3) such that

(η,w)∈C⁡([0,T],X¯2),(\eta,w)\in C([0,T];\overline{X}_{2}),

with f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)). Moreover, for some positive constant C=C⁡(T)C=C(T), we have

‖(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))‖X¯2≤C⁡(‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2+‖(h1,h2)‖L2​(0,T,X−1)),∀t∈[0,T].\displaystyle\|(\eta(t),w(t))\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}\leq C\left(\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}+\|(h_{1},h_{2})\|_{L^{2}(0,T;X_{-1})}\right),\quad\forall t\in[0,T].
Proof.

Firstly, note that if (η,w)∈C⁡([0,T],X¯2)(\eta,w)\in C([0,T];\overline{X}_{2}), we have that

‖Fi​(η,w)‖L2​(0,T)2=∫0T|Fi​(η⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))|2​𝑑t≤C​T​‖Fi‖ℒ⁡(X0,ℝ)2​‖(η,w)‖C⁡([0,T],X¯2)2,\|F_{i}(\eta,w)\|_{L^{2}(0,T)}^{2}=\int_{0}^{T}|F_{i}(\eta(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))|^{2}dt\leq CT\|F_{i}\|_{\mathcal{L}(X_{0};\mathbb{R})}^{2}\|(\eta,w)\|^{2}_{C([0,T];\overline{X}_{2})},

then Fi​(η⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))∈L2​(0,T)F_{i}(\eta(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t))\in L^{2}(0,T), for i=1,2i=1,2.

Let 0<β≤T0<\beta\leq T that will be determinate later. For each (η0,w0)∈X¯2(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in\overline{X}_{2}, consider the map

where, (u,v)(u,v) is the solution of the system (2.3) with f⁡(t)=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t)=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t)=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t)=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)). By Lemma 2.3, the linear map Γ\Gamma is well defined. Furthermore, there exists a positive constant CC, such that

‖Γ⁡(η,w)‖C⁡([0,β],X¯2)≤Cβ​(‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2+‖(F1​(η,w),F2​(η,w))‖[L2​(0,β)]2+‖(h1,h2)‖L2​(0,T,X−1)).\displaystyle\|\Gamma(\eta,w)\|_{C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2})}\leq C_{\beta}(\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}+\|(F_{1}(\eta,w),F_{2}(\eta,w))\|_{[L^{2}(0,\beta)]^{2}}+\|(h_{1},h_{2})\|_{L^{2}(0,T;X_{-1})}).

Then,

‖Γ⁡(η,w)‖C⁡([0,β],X¯2)≤CT​(‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2+‖(h1,h2)‖L2​(0,T,X−1))+CT​β12​(‖F1‖ℒ⁡(X0,ℝ)2+‖F2‖ℒ⁡(X0,ℝ)2)​‖(η,w)‖C⁡([0,β],X¯2).\|\Gamma(\eta,w)\|_{C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2})}\leq C_{T}\left(\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}+\|(h_{1},h_{2})\|_{L^{2}(0,T;X_{-1})}\right)\\ +C_{T}\beta^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\|F_{1}\|_{\mathcal{L}(X_{0};\mathbb{R})}^{2}+\|F_{2}\|_{\mathcal{L}(X_{0};\mathbb{R})}^{2}\right)\|(\eta,w)\|_{C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2})}.

BR​(0):={(η,w)∈C⁡([0,β],X¯2);‖(η,w)‖C⁡([0,β],X¯2)≤R},B_{R}(0):=\{(\eta,w)\in C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2});\|(\eta,w)\|_{C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2})}\leq R\},

≤\displaystyle\leq 12​‖(η1−η2,w1−w2)‖C⁡([0,β],X¯2).\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\|(\eta_{1}-\eta_{2},w_{1}-w_{2})\|_{C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2})}.

‖(η,w)‖C⁡([0,β],X¯2)≤2​CT​(‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2+‖(h1,h2)‖L2​(0,T,X−1)).\displaystyle\|(\eta,w)\|_{C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2})}\leq 2C_{T}\left(\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}+\|(h_{1},h_{2})\|_{L^{2}(0,T;X_{-1})}\right).

Since the choice of β\beta is independent of (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0}), the standard continuation extension argument yields that the solution (η,w)(\eta,w) belongs to C⁡([0,β],X¯2)C([0,\beta];\overline{X}_{2}), thus, the proof is complete. ∎

3. Well-posedness for the stationary system

In this section we are interested to show the well-posedness of the stationary system (1.17)-(1.18). For a better understanding, we recall the definitions of the operators KK and SS:

(3.1) (K​v)​(x):=∫0Lk⁡(x,y)​v​(y)​𝑑yand(S​v)​(x):=∫0Ls⁡(x,y)​v​(y)​𝑑y,for all v∈L2​(0,L),(Kv)(x):=\int_{0}^{L}k(x,y)v(y)dy\quad\text{and}\quad(Sv)(x):=\int_{0}^{L}s(x,y)v(y)dy,\quad\text{for all $v\in L^{2}(0,L)$,}

where (k,s)(k,s) is the solution of stationary problem

(3.2) {ky​y​y+ky+kx​x​x+kx+λ​s=0,in (0,L)×(0,L),sy​y​y+sy+sx​x​x+sx+λ​k=λ​δ​(x−y),in (0,L)×(0,L),\begin{cases}k_{yyy}+k_{y}+k_{xxx}+k_{x}+\lambda s=0,&\text{in $(0,L)\times(0,L)$},\\ s_{yyy}+s_{y}+s_{xxx}+s_{x}+\lambda k=\lambda\delta(x-y),&\text{in $(0,L)\times(0,L)$},\end{cases}

with boundary condition

(3.3) {k⁡(x,0)=k⁡(x,L)=k⁡(0,y)=k⁡(L,y)=ky​(x,0)=ky​(x,L)=0,on (0,L),s⁡(x,0)=s⁡(x,L)=s⁡(0,y)=s⁡(L,y)=sy​(x,0)=sy​(x,L)=0,on (0,L),\left\{\begin{array}[]{l l }k(x,0)=k(x,L)=k(0,y)=k(L,y)=k_{y}(x,0)=k_{y}(x,L)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\\ s(x,0)=s(x,L)=s(0,y)=s(L,y)=s_{y}(x,0)=s_{y}(x,L)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\end{array}\right.

where λ∈ℝ∖{0}\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\} and δ⁡(x−y)\delta(x-y) denotes the Dirac measure on the diagonal of the square [0,L]×[0,L][0,L]\times[0,L].

5. Further comments and open problems

∙\bullet One control on the right end-point

If we consider homogeneous Dirichlet condition and one control inputs at the Neumann boundary condition, then we are not able to prove the rapid stabilization via the backstepping. For instance, if we take g=0g=0, the boundary condition (1.4) becomes

(5.1) {η(0,t)=0,η(L,t)=0,ηx(0,t)=f(t),t∈(0,∞),w(0,t)=0,w(L,t)=0,wx(L,t)=0,t∈(0,∞).\begin{cases}\eta(0,t)=0,\,\,\eta(L,t)=0,\,\,\eta_{x}(0,t)=f(t),&t\in(0,\infty),\\ w(0,t)=0,\,\,w(L,t)=0,\,\,w_{x}(L,t)=0,&t\in(0,\infty).\end{cases}

As we did before, a natural idea is to use the transformation

(5.2) {u⁡(x,t)=η⁡(x,t)−∫0Lk⁡(x,y)​η​(y,t)​𝑑t−∫0Ls⁡(x,y)​w​(y,t)​𝑑yv⁡(x,t)=w⁡(x,t)−∫0Lk⁡(x,y)​w​(y,t)​dy−∫0Ls⁡(x,y)​η​(y,t)​dy,\begin{cases}u(x,t)=\eta(x,t)-\displaystyle\int^{L}_{0}k(x,y)\eta(y,t)dt-\int_{0}^{L}s(x,y)w(y,t)dy\\ v(x,t)=w(x,t)-\displaystyle\int^{L}_{0}k(x,y)w(y,t)dy-\int^{L}_{0}s(x,y)\eta(y,t)dy,\end{cases}

where (k⁡(⋅,⋅),s⁡(⋅,⋅))(k(\cdot,\cdot),s(\cdot,\cdot)) is a solution of an appropriate stationary system. However, it is not clear if that approach, used in this paper, works in this case. Indeed, (5.2) implies that the feedback law will be given by

(5.3) f⁡(t):=F⁡(η,w)=∫0Lkx​(0,y)​η​(y,t)​𝑑t+∫0Lsx​(0,y)​w​(y,t),f(t):=F(\eta,w)=\displaystyle\int^{L}_{0}k_{x}(0,y)\eta(y,t)dt+\int_{0}^{L}s_{x}(0,y)w(y,t),

where (k⁡(⋅,⋅),s⁡(⋅,⋅))(k(\cdot,\cdot),s(\cdot,\cdot)) should solves the stationary system (3.2) with boundary condition (3.3) and a additional restriction

kx​(L,⋅)=sx​(L,⋅)=0.k_{x}(L,\cdot)=s_{x}(L,\cdot)=0.

As in Theorem 3.1, is not difficult to see that the well-posedness of the above stationary problem is equivalent to the well-posedness of the following problem

(5.4) {k¯y​y​y+k¯y+k¯x​x​x+k¯x±λ​k¯=±λ​δ​(x−y)in (0,L)×(0,L),k¯​(x,0)=k¯​(x,L)=0,on (0,L),k¯y​(x,0)=k¯y​(x,L)=0,on (0,L),k¯​(0,y)=k¯​(L,y)=0,on (0,L),k¯x​(L,y)=0,on (0,L),\begin{cases}\overline{k}_{yyy}+\overline{k}_{y}+\overline{k}_{xxx}+\overline{k}_{x}\pm\lambda\overline{k}=\pm\lambda\delta(x-y)&\text{in $(0,L)\times(0,L)$},\\ \overline{k}(x,0)=\overline{k}(x,L)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\\ \overline{k}_{y}(x,0)=\overline{k}_{y}(x,L)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\\ \overline{k}(0,y)=\overline{k}(L,y)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\\ \overline{k}_{x}(L,y)=0,&\text{on $(0,L)$},\end{cases}

for any λ∈ℝ∖{0}\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}. However, with these boundary restrictions the third order system (5.4) becomes over-determined. Therefore, is not clear if such function k¯​(⋅,⋅)\overline{k}(\cdot,\cdot) exists. Thus, the natural open problem appears:

Question 𝒜\mathcal{A}: Can we prove that the nonlinear system (1.14)-(5.1), with f⁡(t)f(t) defined by (5.3), is exponential stable, by using the backstepping method?

∙\bullet Less regularity of the initial data

Consider the following linear KdV-KdV system

(5.5) {ηt+wx+wx​x​x=0,in​(0,L)×(0,+∞),wt+ηx+ηx​x​x=0,in​(0,L)×(0,+∞),η(x,0)=η0(x),w(x,0)=w0(x),in​(0,L),\begin{cases}\eta_{t}+w_{x}+w_{xxx}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,+\infty),\\ w_{t}+\eta_{x}+\eta_{xxx}=0,&\text{in}\,\,(0,L)\times(0,+\infty),\\ \eta(x,0)=\eta_{0}(x),\quad w(x,0)=w_{0}(x),&\text{in}\,\,(0,L),\end{cases}

with following boundary conditions

(5.6) {η(0,t)=0,η(L,t)=0,ηx(0,t)=f(t),on ​(0,T),w(0,t)=0,w(L,t)=0,wx(L,t)=g(t).on ​(0,T),\begin{cases}\eta(0,t)=0,\,\,\eta(L,t)=0,\,\,\eta_{x}(0,t)=f(t),&\text{on }(0,T),\\ w(0,t)=0,\,\,w(L,t)=0,\,\,w_{x}(L,t)=g(t).&\text{on }(0,T),\end{cases}

where f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)), with FiF_{i} in ℒ⁡(X0,ℝ)\mathcal{L}(X_{0};\mathbb{R}), i=1,2i=1,2, defined by (4.1).

When we required less regularity of the initial data, the following result of the well-posedness for the system (5.5)-(5.6) is true:

For every (η0,w0)∈X−1(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in X_{-1} and (f,g)∈[L2​(0,T)]2(f,g)\in[L^{2}(0,T)]^{2}, there exists a unique solution

(η,w)∈C⁡([0,T],X−1)(\eta,w)\in C([0,T];X_{-1})

of system (5.5)-(5.6), such that

‖(η,w)‖L∞​(0,T,X−1)≤C⁡(‖(η0,w0)‖X−1+‖(f,g)‖[L2​(0,T)]2),\displaystyle\|(\eta,w)\|_{L^{\infty}(0,T;X_{-1})}\leq C\left(\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{X_{-1}}+\|(f,g)\|_{[L^{2}(0,T)]^{2}}\right),

for some positive constant C=C⁡(T)C=C(T).

To prove it, we use the classical approach given by the Riesz representation Theorem to obtain a solution by transposition, see [5, 6] for more details. Our analysis on the case of regular data (Theorem 1.1) suggests that is possible to obtain the rapid exponential stabilization for the linear system (5.5) for less regularity of the initial data whenever the linear system is well-posedness in some sense on X0X_{0}. Thus, another natural question arises here is the following one:

Question ℬ\mathcal{B}: Is the linear system (5.5)-(5.6), with f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)) defined by (4.1), well-posedness in X0X_{0} for less regular initial data (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0})?

Due to a lack of a priori X0X_{0}–estimate, the issue of the rapid stabilization for the nonlinear problem is difficult to address. Only when the initial data is regular we can get a positive answer to this question, as was proved in Theorem 1.1. Indeed, in order to obtain a appropriate bound for (4.7), we have to estimate the term −12∫0Lη2(x)wx(x)dx-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{L}\eta^{2}(x)w_{x}(x)dx. This explain why the estimation in the X¯2\overline{X}_{2}-norm it is necessary in our approach. Therefore, for initial data in X0X_{0}, the following question remains open:

Question 𝒞\mathcal{C}: Is the nonlinear system (1.14)-(5.6), with f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)) defined by (4.1), exponential stable for initial data (η0,w0)∈X0(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in X_{0}?

∙\bullet Global well-posedness in time

Adapting the proof of Theorem 2.2, one can also prove that, without any restriction over the initial data (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0}), there exist T∗>0T^{*}>0 and a solution (η,w)(\eta,w) of (1.14)-(1.15), with the feedback law f⁡(t)=F1​(η⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))f(t)=F_{1}(\eta(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t)) and g⁡(t)=F1​(η⁡(⋅,t),w⁡(⋅,t))g(t)=F_{1}(\eta(\cdot,t),w(\cdot,t)) satisfying the initial condition η⁡(⋅,0)=u0​(⋅)\eta(\cdot,0)=u_{0}(\cdot) and w⁡(⋅,0)=w0​(⋅)w(\cdot,0)=w_{0}(\cdot). More precisely,

Theorem 5.1.

Let Fi:X0⟶ℝF_{i}:X_{0}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} be a continuous linear map for i=1,2i=1,2 and the initial data (η0,w0)∈X¯2(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in\overline{X}_{2}. Then, there exists T∗>0T^{*}>0 such that, there exists a unique solution (η,w)∈C⁡([0,T∗],X¯2)(\eta,w)\in C([0,T^{*}];\overline{X}_{2}) of (1.14)-(1.15) with f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)), g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)). Moreover

‖(η,w)‖C⁡([0,T],X¯2)≤C​‖(η0,w0)‖X¯2,\displaystyle\|(\eta,w)\|_{C([0,T];\overline{X}_{2})}\leq C\|(\eta_{0},w_{0})\|_{\overline{X}_{2}},

for some positive constant C=C⁡(T∗)C=C(T^{*}).

Observe that if (η1,w1)∈C⁡([0,T1],X¯2)(\eta_{1},w_{1})\in C([0,T_{1}],\overline{X}_{2}) and (η2,w2)∈C⁡([0,T2],X¯2)(\eta_{2},w_{2})\in C([0,T_{2}],\overline{X}_{2}) are the solutions given by the Theorem 2.2 with initial data (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0}) and (η1​(T1),w1​(T1))(\eta_{1}(T_{1}),w_{1}(T_{1})), respectively, the function (η,w):[0,T1+T2]→X¯2(\eta,w):[0,T_{1}+T_{2}]\rightarrow\overline{X}_{2} defined by

(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))={(η1​(t),w1​(t))if t∈[0,T1],(η2​(t−T1),w2​(t−T2))if t∈[T1,T1+T2],\displaystyle(\eta(t),w(t))=\begin{cases}(\eta_{1}(t),w_{1}(t))&\text{if $t\in[0,T_{1}]$},\\ (\eta_{2}(t-T_{1}),w_{2}(t-T_{2}))&\text{if $t\in[T_{1},T_{1}+T_{2}]$},\end{cases}

is the solution of the feedback system on interval [0,T1+T2][0,T_{1}+T_{2}] with initial data (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0}). This argument allows us extend a local solution until a maximal interval, that is, for all 0<T<Tmax≤∞0<T<T_{\max}\leq\infty there exist a function (η,w)∈C⁡([0,T],X¯2)(\eta,w)\in C([0,T],\overline{X}_{2}) solution of the feedback system (1.14)-(1.15). The following proposition, easily holds:

Proposition 5.2.

Let (η0,w0)∈X¯2(\eta_{0},w_{0})\in\overline{X}_{2} and (η,w)∈C⁡([0,T],X¯2)(\eta,w)\in C([0,T],\overline{X}_{2}) solution of the feedback system, for all 0<T<Tmax0<T<T_{\max}, with initial data (η0,w0)(\eta_{0},w_{0}). Then, only one of the following assertions hold:

  1. (i)

    Tmax=∞T_{\max}=\infty;

  2. (ii)

    If Tmax<∞T_{\max}<\infty, then, limt→Tmax‖(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))‖X¯2=∞\lim_{t\rightarrow T_{\max}}\|(\eta(t),w(t))\|_{\overline{X}_{2}}=\infty.

Thus, the following questions related to the global well-posedness in time are also important:

Question 𝒟\mathcal{D}: Let Fi:X0⟶ℝF_{i}:X_{0}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} be a continuous linear map for i=1,2i=1,2. Is the nonlinear system (1.14)-(1.15), with f⁡(t):=F1​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))f(t):=F_{1}(\eta(t),w(t)) and g⁡(t):=F2​(η⁡(t),w⁡(t))g(t):=F_{2}(\eta(t),w(t)), global well-posedness in time, i.e, TmaxT_{\max} is infinity?

Question ℰ\mathcal{E}: If the question 𝒟\mathcal{D} has positive answer, do have expect some restriction on the initial data?

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:
